name: Group cancellation
statement: In a group, left and right cancellation are valid: if ab=ac then b=c, and if ba=ca then b=c.

typical_uses: Cancel a common factor from both sides of a group equation.

common_misuses: Cancelling in a structure not known to be a group or cancellative monoid.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule

statement: Every subgroup of the additive group of integers is either {0} or dZ for a unique positive integer d.

typical_uses: Classify kernels or images of homomorphisms involving Z.

common_misuses: Assuming a least positive element exists without first showing the subgroup is nonzero.

conclusion: There exist integers r,s with d=ra+sb.
typical_uses: Prove relative primality statements.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Orbit-stabilizer counting formula
statement: For a finite group action, the size of the group equals the size of an orbit times the size of the stabilizer of any point in that orbit.
conditions: A finite group G acts on a set S
s is in S
conclusion: |G|=|Orbit(s)|*|Stab(s)|.
typical_uses: Count orbits, stabilizers, and conjugacy classes.
Prove divisibility facts for group actions.
common_misuses: Using the formula for nonfinite sets without a finite counting version.
Confusing stabilizer of a point with kernel of the whole action.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Class equation
statement: A finite group is partitioned into conjugacy classes, and each conjugacy class has size equal to the index of the centralizer of any element in it.
conditions: G is a finite group
conclusion: |G| is the sum of sizes of conjugacy classes; |C_G(x)|*[conjugacy_class_size_of_x]=|G|.
typical_uses: Study centers and normal subgroups.
Prove results about p-groups and simple groups.
common_misuses: Confusing centralizer with center.
Assuming all conjugacy classes have the same size.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Center of a p-group
statement: Every nontrivial finite p-group has nontrivial center.
conditions: G is a finite group of order p^n with n>=1
conclusion: Z(G) is not trivial.
typical_uses: Prove groups of order p^2 are abelian.
Start induction arguments on p-groups.
common_misuses: Applying to groups whose order is not a prime power.
Concluding the whole group is abelian from nontrivial center alone.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Sylow theorems
statement: If |G|=p^e m with p not dividing m, then Sylow p-subgroups exist, are conjugate, every p-subgroup lies in one, and the number s of Sylow p-subgroups divides m and satisfies s=1 mod p.
conditions: G is a finite group
p is prime
|G|=p^e m with p not dividing m
conclusion: Sylow p-subgroups exist and satisfy conjugacy and counting constraints.
typical_uses: Classify small finite groups.
Prove normality when the Sylow count must be 1.
common_misuses: Assuming a Sylow subgroup is always normal.
Forgetting both constraints on the number of Sylow subgroups.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Conjugacy in symmetric groups
statement: Two permutations in S_n are conjugate if and only if their cycle decompositions have the same cycle lengths.
conditions: p and q are permutations in S_n
conclusion: p and q are conjugate exactly when they have the same cycle type.
typical_uses: Compute conjugacy classes in symmetric groups.
Analyze normal subgroups via unions of conjugacy classes.
common_misuses: Using cycle type for conjugacy inside A_n without checking whether the S_n class splits.
Ignoring fixed points in cycle type.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Substitution principle
statement: A ring homomorphism from a polynomial ring is determined by the image of the coefficient ring and the chosen images of the variables.
conditions: R[x_1,...,x_n] is a polynomial ring
a target ring and compatible images for coefficients and variables are specified
conclusion: There is a unique homomorphism extending the coefficient map and sending each variable to its chosen image.
typical_uses: Define evaluation maps.
Identify kernels of substitution homomorphisms.
common_misuses: Assuming arbitrary assignments define homomorphisms when coefficient maps are incompatible.
Forgetting uniqueness depends on the universal property of polynomial rings.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Adjoining a root by quotient
statement: If f is a monic polynomial over R, then in R[x]/(f), the class of x is a formal root of f and every element has a representative of degree less than deg(f).
conditions: f is monic of positive degree in R[x]
conclusion: R[x]/(f) adjoins an element alpha with f(alpha)=0 and has normal forms of bounded degree.
typical_uses: Construct extension rings or fields.
Reduce polynomial expressions modulo f.
common_misuses: Assuming the quotient is a field without f irreducible over a field.
Forgetting normal forms require f to be monic for general rings.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Irreducible polynomial of an algebraic element
statement: For an algebraic element alpha over F, its irreducible polynomial is the unique monic polynomial of least degree in F[x] with alpha as a root; it divides every polynomial in F[x] that vanishes at alpha.
conditions: K/F is a field extension
alpha in K is algebraic over F
conclusion: There is a unique irreducible polynomial m_alpha,F with the stated divisibility property.
typical_uses: Show two elements have the same algebraic type over F.
Identify kernels of evaluation maps F[x]->K.
common_misuses: Changing the base field without recomputing irreducibility.
Using a reducible polynomial as a minimal polynomial.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Adjoining algebraic elements gives a field
statement: If alpha is algebraic over F with irreducible polynomial f, then F[alpha]=F(alpha) and F[alpha] is isomorphic to F[x]/(f).
conditions: alpha is algebraic over F
f is the irreducible polynomial of alpha over F
conclusion: F[alpha] is already a field and is F-isomorphic to F[x]/(f).
typical_uses: Represent elements of simple algebraic extensions.
Prove quotient fields from irreducible polynomials.
common_misuses: Assuming F[alpha]=F(alpha) for transcendental alpha.
Forgetting f must be irreducible over F.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Basis of a simple algebraic extension
statement: If alpha has irreducible polynomial of degree n over F, then 1,alpha,...,alpha^{n-1} is an F-basis of F(alpha).
conditions: alpha is algebraic over F
deg m_alpha,F = n
conclusion: [F(alpha):F]=n and powers below n form a basis.
typical_uses: Compute extension degrees.
Write elements uniquely in a simple extension.
common_misuses: Including alpha^n in the basis.
Using powers as a basis before proving the polynomial degree.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Tower law for field degrees
statement: For finite extensions F subset L subset K, [K:F]=[K:L][L:F].
conditions: F subset L subset K are fields
K/L and L/F are finite extensions
conclusion: Field degrees multiply in towers.
typical_uses: Compute extension degrees.
Rule out possible intermediate fields.
common_misuses: Adding degrees instead of multiplying.
Applying when one extension degree is infinite without care.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: F-isomorphisms preserve polynomial roots
statement: An F-isomorphism sends roots of polynomials with coefficients in F to roots of the same polynomials.
conditions: sigma:K->K' is an F-isomorphism
f is in F[x]
alpha in K
f(alpha)=0
conclusion: f(sigma(alpha))=0.
typical_uses: Constrain possible field automorphisms.
Find images of algebraic generators.
common_misuses: Applying to polynomials whose coefficients are not fixed by the isomorphism.
Assuming every root image remains in the original field if the isomorphism maps to a different extension.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Uniqueness of splitting fields
statement: Any two splitting fields of a polynomial over F are F-isomorphic.
conditions: f is a polynomial over F
K and L are splitting fields of f over F
conclusion: K and L are isomorphic as extensions of F.
typical_uses: Work with a chosen splitting field without loss of generality.
Show Galois groups are well-defined up to isomorphism.
common_misuses: Assuming the isomorphism is unique without specifying images of roots.
Forgetting the isomorphism must fix F.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Fixed field theorem
statement: If H is a finite group of automorphisms of K and F is its fixed field, then K/F is finite and [K:F]=|H|.
conditions: H is a finite group of automorphisms of field K
F=K^H
conclusion: K is a finite extension of F with degree equal to |H|.
typical_uses: Compute degrees from automorphism groups.
Prove an element lies in the fixed field.
common_misuses: Using the theorem for infinite automorphism groups without the finite hypothesis.
Confusing fixed field K^H with the base field in a non-Galois extension.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Characterizations of Galois extensions
statement: For a finite extension K/F with Galois group G, the following are equivalent: |G|=[K:F], the fixed field K^G is F, and K is a splitting field over F.
conditions: K/F is a finite field extension
G is the group of F-automorphisms of K
conclusion: The listed conditions characterize when K/F is Galois.
typical_uses: Prove an extension is Galois.
Move between splitting-field and automorphism-count arguments.
common_misuses: Calling an arbitrary finite extension Galois without checking one of the equivalent conditions.
Assuming all roots of all polynomials over F lie in K.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Basis change for bilinear forms
statement: If A is the matrix of a bilinear form in one basis and the basis changes by P, then the new matrix is P^t A P.
conditions: A represents a bilinear form
P is an invertible change-of-basis matrix
conclusion: The form matrix transforms by congruence, not similarity.
typical_uses: Distinguish operator matrices from form matrices.
Check correct basis-change formulas for quadratic and bilinear forms.
common_misuses: Using P^{-1}AP for a bilinear form.
Treating congruent matrices as similar matrices.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Positive definite symmetric forms
statement: A real matrix represents dot product in some basis if and only if it is symmetric and positive definite; equivalently it has the form P^t P for some invertible P.
conditions: A is a real n by n matrix
conclusion: A is congruent to the identity iff A is symmetric positive definite iff A=P^tP for invertible P.
typical_uses: Recognize positive definite forms.
Repair arguments that confuse positive determinant with positive definiteness.
common_misuses: Assuming symmetric alone implies positive definite.
Checking only det(A)>0 instead of all required positivity conditions.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Basis change for Hermitian forms
statement: If A is the matrix of a Hermitian form and the basis changes by P, then the new matrix is P^* A P.
conditions: A represents a Hermitian form
P is an invertible complex change-of-basis matrix
conclusion: Hermitian form matrices transform by A' = P^* A P.
typical_uses: Check unitary and Hermitian computations.
Avoid using transpose instead of conjugate transpose.
common_misuses: Using P^tAP instead of P^*AP over complex vector spaces.
Using similarity P^{-1}AP for a form.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Hermitian eigenvalues are real
statement: The eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix are real. Consequently the trace and determinant of a Hermitian matrix are real.
conditions: A is a Hermitian matrix
conclusion: Every eigenvalue of A is real.
typical_uses: Justify real spectral data for Hermitian and real symmetric matrices.
Detect impossible nonreal eigenvalue claims.
common_misuses: Applying the result to arbitrary complex matrices.
Forgetting that real symmetric matrices are Hermitian only after viewing them over C.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Unitary matrix criterion
statement: A complex matrix P is unitary exactly when P^*P=I; equivalently its columns form an orthonormal basis for the standard Hermitian form.
conditions: P is a square complex matrix
conclusion: P is unitary iff P^*P=I iff its columns are orthonormal.
typical_uses: Verify a unitary diagonalization.
Check preservation of the standard Hermitian form.
common_misuses: Using P^tP=I over complex scalars.
Assuming columns of norm one are enough without pairwise orthogonality.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Nondegenerate form matrix criterion
statement: A symmetric or Hermitian form is nondegenerate if and only if its matrix in any basis is invertible; null vectors correspond to solutions of AY=0.
conditions: A is the matrix of a symmetric or Hermitian form in a basis
conclusion: The form is nondegenerate iff det(A) != 0.
typical_uses: Check nondegeneracy by determinant.
Find the nullspace of a form.
common_misuses: Confusing nondegenerate with positive definite.
Checking invertibility in only one basis but using the wrong basis-change formula.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Orthogonal decomposition by nondegenerate subspace
statement: If a symmetric or Hermitian form is nondegenerate on a subspace W, then V is the direct sum of W and W^perp.
conditions: W is a subspace of V
the form is nondegenerate on W
conclusion: V = W direct_sum W^perp.
typical_uses: Split a space into orthogonal pieces.
Prove existence and uniqueness of orthogonal projections.
common_misuses: Assuming V=W direct_sum W^perp when the restriction to W is degenerate.
Using positive-definite intuition for indefinite forms without checking nondegeneracy.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Projection formula
statement: For an orthogonal basis, the component of a vector along a basis vector v is scaled by (v,w)/(v,v), provided (v,v) is nonzero.
conditions: B is an orthogonal basis
v is a basis vector with (v,v) != 0
conclusion: Orthogonal coordinates are computed by inner products divided by self-products.
typical_uses: Compute projections in orthogonal bases.
Check missing nonzero denominator conditions.
common_misuses: Using the formula with a null vector where (v,v)=0.
Using it for a nonorthogonal basis without solving a linear system.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Positive definite principal minor criterion
statement: A real symmetric matrix is positive definite if and only if its leading principal minors all have positive determinant.
conditions: A is a real symmetric matrix
A_k denotes the leading k by k principal submatrix
conclusion: A is positive definite iff det(A_k)>0 for every k.
typical_uses: Test positive definiteness.
Repair proofs that use only the full determinant.
common_misuses: Checking principal minors without symmetry.
Checking only det(A)>0.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Spectral theorem for normal operators
statement: A normal operator on a finite-dimensional Hermitian space has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors; equivalently a normal matrix is unitarily diagonalizable.
conditions: T is a normal operator on a finite-dimensional Hermitian space
conclusion: There is an orthonormal eigenbasis for T.
typical_uses: Diagonalize unitary and Hermitian operators.
Justify orthogonal eigenspace decompositions.
common_misuses: Applying the theorem to nonnormal matrices.
Confusing diagonalizable with unitarily diagonalizable.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Spectral theorem for Hermitian operators
statement: A Hermitian operator has an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors and all eigenvalues are real.
conditions: T is Hermitian on a finite-dimensional Hermitian space
conclusion: T is unitarily diagonalizable with real diagonal entries.
typical_uses: Diagonalize Hermitian matrices.
Prove quadratic form properties from eigenvalues.
common_misuses: Assuming every diagonalizable complex matrix is Hermitian.
Forgetting orthonormality is part of the conclusion.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Spectral theorem for real symmetric operators
statement: A real symmetric matrix is orthogonally diagonalizable and has real eigenvalues.
conditions: A is a real symmetric matrix
conclusion: There is an orthogonal P such that P^t A P is diagonal with real entries.
typical_uses: Diagonalize quadratic forms and symmetric operators.
Prove real eigenvalue claims.
common_misuses: Using orthogonal diagonalization for nonsymmetric real matrices.
Replacing P^tAP with P^{-1}AP without noting that P^{-1}=P^t for orthogonal P.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Nondegenerate skew-symmetric forms have even dimension
statement: A vector space with a nondegenerate skew-symmetric form has even dimension, and the form has a basis with standard 2 by 2 skew blocks.
conditions: V has a nondegenerate skew-symmetric bilinear form
conclusion: dim(V) is even and the form has standard symplectic block matrix.
typical_uses: Rule out nondegenerate skew forms in odd dimension.
Put a skew form into normal form.
common_misuses: Assuming orthogonal bases exist for skew-symmetric forms.
Ignoring characteristic 2 issues.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: First isomorphism theorem for modules
statement: If f:V->W is a module homomorphism with kernel K, then V/K is isomorphic to im(f). If f is surjective, then V/K is isomorphic to W.
conditions: f:V->W is an R-module homomorphism
K=ker(f)
conclusion: V/K ~= im(f), and if f is onto then V/K ~= W.
typical_uses: Identify quotient modules.
Repair module proofs that skip kernel quotient arguments.
common_misuses: Using a quotient by a subset that is not a submodule.
Claiming the quotient equals W without surjectivity.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Correspondence theorem for modules
statement: For a surjective module homomorphism f:V->Vbar with kernel W, submodules of Vbar correspond to submodules of V containing W.
conditions: f:V->Vbar is a surjective R-module homomorphism
W=ker(f)
conclusion: Submodules of Vbar are in bijection with submodules S of V such that W subset S.
typical_uses: Analyze submodules of quotient modules.
Lift quotient-module questions to the original module.
common_misuses: Forgetting the containing-kernel condition.
Applying the correspondence to a nonsurjective map without replacing the codomain by the image.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Free module basis criterion
statement: An R-module is free if and only if it has a basis; equivalently it is isomorphic to R^n for some n.
conditions: V is an R-module
conclusion: V is free iff elements of V have unique coordinate expressions in some generating set.
typical_uses: Decide when matrix-coordinate methods apply to modules.
Detect invalid vector-space-style arguments for nonfree modules.
common_misuses: Assuming every finitely generated module is free.
Assuming every spanning set in a module contains a basis.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Invertible matrices over a ring
statement: For a square matrix over a nonzero commutative ring, invertibility implies and is implied by its determinant being a unit.
conditions: R is a nonzero commutative ring
A is a square R-matrix
conclusion: A is invertible over R iff det(A) is a unit in R.
typical_uses: Check invertibility over Z or polynomial rings.
Avoid treating nonzero determinant as enough over a ring.
common_misuses: Using det(A) != 0 instead of det(A) being a unit over a general ring.
Using a real inverse for an integer matrix and claiming it is invertible over Z.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Change of basis in free modules
statement: A change-of-basis matrix in a free module over a nonzero ring is invertible, and any two bases have the same cardinality.
conditions: V is a free R-module
R is not the zero ring
conclusion: Basis changes are given by invertible R-matrices and rank is well-defined.
typical_uses: Justify rank of a free module.
Check whether a proposed basis change is valid over a ring.
common_misuses: Using a matrix with nonunit determinant as a basis change over Z.
Assuming real invertibility implies R-invertibility.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Noetherian ring and ascending chain condition
statement: A ring is noetherian if every ideal is finitely generated; equivalently it has no infinite strictly increasing chain of ideals.
conditions: R is a ring
conclusion: Noetherianity can be checked by finite generation of ideals or by the ascending chain condition.
typical_uses: Prove termination of ideal/module constructions.
Find missing finite-generation assumptions.
common_misuses: Using descending chains instead of ascending chains.
Assuming every ring is noetherian.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Submodules over noetherian rings
statement: Over a noetherian ring, every submodule of a finitely generated module is finitely generated.
conditions: R is a noetherian ring
V is a finitely generated R-module
W is a submodule of V
conclusion: W is finitely generated.
typical_uses: Prove relation modules are finitely generated.
Justify finite presentations in noetherian settings.
common_misuses: Dropping the noetherian hypothesis.
Assuming submodules of finitely generated modules are finitely generated over arbitrary rings.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Hilbert basis theorem
statement: If R is noetherian, then the polynomial ring R[x] is noetherian; by induction, so is R[x_1,...,x_n].
conditions: R is a noetherian ring
conclusion: Polynomial rings in finitely many variables over R are noetherian.
typical_uses: Show ideals in polynomial rings are finitely generated.
Support algebraic geometry quotient-ring arguments.
common_misuses: Applying to infinitely many variables without extra hypotheses.
Assuming quotient or localization results without proving them separately.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Structure theorem for finitely generated abelian groups
statement: Every finitely generated abelian group is a direct sum of finite cyclic groups with invariant factors d_i>1 and d_i dividing d_{i+1}, together with a free abelian group.
conditions: V is a finitely generated abelian group
conclusion: V ~= C_{d1} direct_sum ... direct_sum C_{dk} direct_sum Z^r with d_i | d_{i+1}.
typical_uses: Classify finitely generated abelian groups.
Identify torsion and free parts.
common_misuses: Assuming arbitrary nonabelian groups decompose this way.
Forgetting the divisibility condition in invariant-factor form.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Finite abelian prime-power decomposition
statement: Every finite abelian group is a direct sum of cyclic groups of prime-power order.
conditions: V is a finite abelian group
conclusion: V decomposes as a direct sum of cyclic p-power groups.
typical_uses: Classify finite abelian groups by prime power factors.
Count possible abelian groups of a given order.
common_misuses: Assuming the decomposition applies to nonabelian finite groups.
Ignoring uniqueness issues when comparing decompositions.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Constructible numbers have degree a power of two
statement: A constructible real number lies in a tower of real quadratic extensions over Q, so its degree over Q is a power of two.
conditions: a is a constructible real number
conclusion: a is algebraic over Q and deg_Q(a) is a power of 2.
typical_uses: Prove impossibility of ruler-and-compass constructions.
Rule out constructibility by degree.
common_misuses: Using degree a power of two as a sufficient condition without additional hypotheses.
Forgetting the number must be real constructible.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Adjoining a root via irreducible quotient
statement: If f is irreducible over a field F, then F[x]/(f) is a field that contains a formal root of f.
conditions: F is a field
f is an irreducible polynomial in F[x]
conclusion: F[x]/(f) is a field extension of F in which the class of x is a root of f.
typical_uses: Construct finite field extensions.
Build examples by adjoining roots.
common_misuses: Assuming F[x]/(f) is a field when f is reducible.
Forgetting the root is the residue class of x, not an element of F.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Main facts about finite fields
statement: For q=p^r, a field of order q exists and is unique up to isomorphism; its elements are the roots of x^q-x; its multiplicative group is cyclic of order q-1; it contains a subfield of order p^k iff k divides r.
conditions: p is prime
q=p^r
conclusion: Finite fields of order q are classified and satisfy the listed root, cyclicity, and subfield properties.
typical_uses: Compute finite field elements and subfields.
Use cyclicity of finite field units.
common_misuses: Assuming a field exists for every finite order not a prime power.
Confusing F_q with Z/qZ when q is not prime.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Frobenius additivity
statement: In characteristic p, for q=p^r, (x+y)^q=x^q+y^q.
conditions: The field or ring has characteristic p
q=p^r
conclusion: The qth power map is additive in characteristic p.
typical_uses: Show roots of x^q-x form a subfield.
Check finite field closure under addition.
common_misuses: Using the formula in characteristic zero.
Using (x+y)^n=x^n+y^n when n is not a p-power in characteristic p.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Primitive element theorem in characteristic zero
statement: Every finite extension of a field of characteristic zero has a primitive element.
conditions: K/F is a finite field extension
char(F)=0
conclusion: There exists alpha in K such that K=F(alpha).
typical_uses: Reduce finite extensions to simple extensions.
Use one generator for automorphism and minimal polynomial arguments.
common_misuses: Applying the characteristic-zero version to arbitrary positive-characteristic extensions.
Assuming a specific linear combination is primitive without excluding bad parameters.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Galois group action on roots
statement: If K/F is Galois and a polynomial over F splits in K, then the Galois group permutes its roots; if K is the splitting field, this action is faithful, and if the polynomial is irreducible, the action is transitive.
conditions: K/F is Galois
g in F[x] splits in K
conclusion: G(K/F) acts on the root set, with faithfulness for splitting fields and transitivity for irreducible g.
typical_uses: Embed Galois groups into symmetric groups.
Analyze irreducible polynomial Galois groups.
common_misuses: Assuming the action is faithful when K is larger than the splitting field generated by those roots.
Assuming transitivity for reducible polynomials.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Main theorem of Galois theory
statement: For a Galois extension K/F with Galois group G, subgroups H of G correspond bijectively to intermediate fields L via H -> K^H and L -> G(K/L).
conditions: K/F is a Galois extension
G=G(K/F)
conclusion: Subgroups of G and intermediate fields between F and K are in inclusion-reversing bijection.
typical_uses: List intermediate fields from subgroup data.
Translate field-degree questions into subgroup-index questions.
common_misuses: Using the correspondence for non-Galois extensions.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Degrees in the Galois correspondence
statement: If L corresponds to H under the Galois correspondence for K/F, then [K:L]=|H| and [L:F]=[G:H].
conditions: K/F is Galois with group G
L is an intermediate field
H=G(K/L)
conclusion: Field degrees equal subgroup order and index as stated.
typical_uses: Compute intermediate field degrees.
Rule out intermediate fields from subgroup indices.
common_misuses: Reversing |H| and [G:H].
Using subgroup counts without checking the extension is Galois.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Normal subgroups and Galois intermediate fields
statement: In a Galois extension K/F, an intermediate field L is Galois over F if and only if the corresponding subgroup H=G(K/L) is normal in G; then G(L/F) is isomorphic to G/H.
conditions: K/F is Galois with group G
L corresponds to H
conclusion: L/F is Galois iff H normal in G, and then G(L/F) ~= G/H.
typical_uses: Identify normal intermediate extensions.
Compute quotient Galois groups.

Using G/H when H is not normal.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Irreducible cubic Galois group by discriminant

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Prime cyclotomic Galois group

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Jordan decomposition over C

conclusion: T has a Jordan form, unique up to ordering of Jordan blocks.
typical_uses: Reduce complex matrix questions to Jordan blocks.
Diagnose invalid diagonalization by replacing it with Jordan form.
common_misuses: Assuming the same theorem over a field where the characteristic polynomial does not split.
Claiming the Jordan basis is canonical rather than the block data up to order.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Jordan block sizes from kernels
statement: For a fixed eigenvalue lambda, the dimensions of ker((T-lambda I)^i) determine how many Jordan blocks for lambda have size at least i.
conditions: The characteristic polynomial splits
lambda is an eigenvalue of T
conclusion: dim ker((T-lambda I)^i)-dim ker((T-lambda I)^{i-1}) counts the number of lambda-blocks of size at least i.
typical_uses: Determine possible Jordan forms from kernel dimensions.
Catch errors that confuse algebraic and geometric multiplicity.
common_misuses: Using only ker(T-lambda I) to determine all block sizes.
Mixing kernel counts for different eigenvalues.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Diagonalizable iff Jordan blocks are size one
statement: A complex linear operator is diagonalizable if and only if every generalized eigenvector is an eigenvector, equivalently all Jordan blocks have size 1.
conditions: T is a linear operator on a finite-dimensional complex vector space
conclusion: T is diagonalizable iff its Jordan form has only 1 by 1 blocks.
typical_uses: Test diagonalizability with generalized eigenspaces.
Explain why repeated eigenvalues need not prevent diagonalization.
common_misuses: Assuming a split characteristic polynomial is enough for diagonalizability.
Assuming repeated roots always imply non-diagonalizability.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Finite-order operators are diagonalizable when roots split
statement: If T^r=I and t^r-1 splits into distinct linear factors over the base field, then T is diagonalizable. In characteristic zero over C this always applies.
conditions: T is a linear operator
T^r=I for some r>=1
t^r-1 splits into distinct linear factors over the base field
conclusion: T is diagonalizable.
typical_uses: Diagonalize finite group actions over C.
Repair proofs that need semisimplicity of finite-order operators.
common_misuses: Ignoring characteristic p cases where t^r-1 may have repeated roots.
Assuming T^r=0 gives diagonalizability.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Smith normal form over Z
statement: Every integer matrix can be transformed by invertible integer row and column operations into a diagonal matrix with positive diagonal entries d_1,...,d_k satisfying d_i divides d_{i+1}.
conditions: A is an integer m by n matrix
conclusion: There exist P in GL_n(Z) and Q in GL_m(Z) such that Q^{-1}AP is diagonal with invariant factors d_i.
typical_uses: Solve integer linear systems.
Classify finitely generated abelian groups from presentations.
common_misuses: Using rational row reduction instead of unimodular integer operations.
Forgetting the divisibility condition on invariant factors.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Integer kernels from Smith normal form
statement: If A'=Q^{-1}AP is the Smith diagonal form of A, then integer solutions of AX=0 are exactly X=P X' where A'X'=0.
conditions: A is an integer matrix
A'=Q^{-1}AP is Smith diagonal
P and Q are unimodular integer matrices
conclusion: The kernel over Z is transported from the diagonal system by P.
typical_uses: Find a Z-basis for homogeneous integer solutions.
Check whether a proof incorrectly solves over Q or R.
common_misuses: Using arbitrary invertible rational matrices for P or Q.
Forgetting to transform solutions back by P.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Integer images from Smith normal form
statement: If A'=Q^{-1}AP is Smith diagonal with diagonal entries d_i, then im(A') is generated over Z by d_i e_i, and im(A) is obtained by applying Q to this image.
conditions: A is an integer matrix
A'=Q^{-1}AP is Smith diagonal
conclusion: Y lies in im_Z(A) iff Q^{-1}Y lies in the subgroup generated by the nonzero d_i e_i.
typical_uses: Decide solvability of AX=B over Z.
Compute quotient groups Z^m/im(A).
common_misuses: Checking only real rank for integer solvability.
Forgetting divisibility conditions imposed by the diagonal entries.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Subgroups of free abelian groups are free
statement: Every subgroup of a free abelian group of finite rank is itself free abelian with rank no larger than the ambient rank.
conditions: W is a free abelian group of finite rank
U is a subgroup of W
conclusion: U is free abelian and rank(U)<=rank(W).
typical_uses: Justify bases for sublattices and kernels in Z^n.
Repair proofs that assume subgroup generators are independent without argument.
common_misuses: Applying this to nonabelian groups.
Assuming the same statement for arbitrary modules over arbitrary rings.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Relations from a presentation matrix
statement: If V=R^m/AR^n is presented by the matrix A, the images of the standard basis generate V, and a linear combination BY is zero exactly when Y is in the column span of A.
conditions: A is an m by n matrix over R
V=R^m/AR^n
conclusion: Relations among the m generators are precisely R-linear combinations of the columns of A.
typical_uses: Translate generators and relations into matrices.
Diagnose missing relation checks in module or abelian group proofs.
common_misuses: Putting relation vectors as rows when the convention uses columns.
Treating a non-complete relation set as complete.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Quotients of noetherian rings
statement: A quotient of a noetherian ring is noetherian. Hence any quotient of a polynomial ring in finitely many variables over Z or over a field is noetherian.
conditions: R is noetherian
I is an ideal of R
conclusion: R/I is noetherian.
typical_uses: Show finitely generated algebra quotients have finitely generated ideals.
Justify finite presentations after imposing polynomial relations.
common_misuses: Assuming subrings of noetherian rings are automatically noetherian.
Forgetting the finite-variable condition for polynomial rings.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Uniqueness of finite abelian prime-power decomposition
statement: In the decomposition of a finite abelian group into cyclic groups of prime-power order, the occurring prime powers are uniquely determined by the group.
conditions: V is a finite abelian group
V is decomposed as a direct sum of cyclic prime-power groups
conclusion: The multiset of cyclic prime-power orders is an invariant of V.
typical_uses: Prove two finite abelian groups are not isomorphic.
Count isomorphism classes of finite abelian groups.
common_misuses: Comparing only the total order of the groups.
Using the theorem for nonabelian groups.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Smith normal form over F[t]
statement: For R=F[t], every matrix over R can be diagonalized by elementary invertible R-matrix operations so that the nonzero diagonal entries are monic and divide successively.
conditions: F is a field
A is a matrix over F[t]
conclusion: A has a Smith normal form over F[t] with monic invariant factors.
typical_uses: Classify finitely generated F[t]-modules.
Derive rational canonical forms of linear operators.
common_misuses: Applying the statement to multivariable polynomial rings.
Forgetting to make invariant factors monic.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Linear operators as F[t]-modules
statement: A linear operator T on an F-vector space V makes V into an F[t]-module by letting t act as T; submodules are exactly T-invariant subspaces.
conditions: T is a linear operator on an F-vector space V
conclusion: F[t]-module structure encodes the action of T and its invariant subspaces.
typical_uses: Translate operator classification into module classification.
Recognize cyclic subspaces generated by v,Tv,T^2v,...
common_misuses: Forgetting that scalar multiplication by t is not ordinary scalar multiplication in F.
Treating all F[t]-modules as free over F[t].

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Rational canonical form from invariant factors
statement: The Smith normal form of the F[t]-module associated to a linear operator yields a block form over F, the rational canonical form, built from cyclic modules F[t]/(f_i).
conditions: T is a linear operator on a finite-dimensional F-vector space
The associated F[t]-module has invariant factors f_i
conclusion: T is similar over F to the direct sum of companion-type blocks determined by the f_i.
typical_uses: Classify linear operators without splitting eigenvalues.
Distinguish similarity over F from diagonalization over an algebraic closure.
common_misuses: Replacing rational canonical form by Jordan form over a field where eigenvalues need not lie.
Ignoring invariant-factor divisibility.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Change of basis for representations
statement: Changing the basis of a representation conjugates every representing matrix by the same invertible matrix.
conditions: R is a matrix representation of G
P is a change-of-basis matrix
conclusion: The new representation is R'_g=P^{-1}R_gP for every g in G.
typical_uses: Check whether two matrix representations are isomorphic.
Avoid changing basis separately for different group elements.
common_misuses: Using a different P for different g when claiming representation equivalence.
Confusing equality of matrices with isomorphism of representations.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: G-invariant subspaces and direct sums
statement: A subspace W of a representation V is G-invariant if every group element maps W into W; a decomposition into G-invariant subspaces gives a direct-sum representation with block diagonal matrices in a compatible basis.
conditions: p is a representation of G on V
V is a direct sum of G-invariant subspaces
conclusion: The representation decomposes as the direct sum of its restrictions.
typical_uses: Detect reducibility from invariant subspaces.
Explain block diagonal matrix representations.
common_misuses: Using an arbitrary vector-space direct sum whose summands are not G-invariant.
Expecting block diagonal form in a basis not adapted to the decomposition.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Maschke theorem for finite complex representations
statement: Every finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group is a direct sum of irreducible representations.
conditions: G is finite
V is a nonzero finite-dimensional complex representation of G
conclusion: V decomposes into irreducible subrepresentations.
typical_uses: Reduce character and representation questions to irreducibles.
Remove upper-right junk blocks by choosing a better invariant complement.
common_misuses: Applying the theorem in positive characteristic dividing |G| without extra hypotheses.
Assuming a chosen invariant subspace automatically has an arbitrary complement invariant.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Finite group representations are unitarizable over C
statement: Every finite-dimensional complex representation of a finite group admits a G-invariant positive definite Hermitian form, so in a suitable basis all representing matrices are unitary.
conditions: G is finite
p:G->GL(V) is a complex representation
conclusion: p is equivalent to a unitary representation.
typical_uses: Use orthogonal complements as invariant complements.
Prove Maschke theorem by averaging an inner product.
common_misuses: Assuming the original basis already gives unitary matrices.
Dropping finiteness when using finite averaging over G.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Character dimension and conjugacy invariance
statement: The character of a representation is chi(g)=trace(rho_g). It satisfies chi(1)=dim V and is constant on conjugacy classes.
conditions: rho is a finite-dimensional representation of G
conclusion: chi is a class function and its value at the identity is the representation dimension.
typical_uses: Build character tables.
Check impossible proposed characters.
common_misuses: Treating higher-dimensional characters as homomorphisms.
Forgetting trace is invariant under conjugation.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Irreducible character orthogonality
statement: For a finite group, irreducible characters are orthonormal under the standard class-function inner product, and any character decomposes as an integer sum of irreducible characters using these inner products as multiplicities.
conditions: G is finite
Characters are complex characters of G
conclusion: The multiplicity of irreducible chi_i in chi is <chi,chi_i>.
typical_uses: Decompose representations from character values.
Test irreducibility by computing <chi,chi>.
common_misuses: Using ordinary dot product without class sizes or the 1/|G| factor.
Expecting non-character class functions to have nonnegative integer coefficients.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Irreducible characters of finite abelian groups
statement: Every irreducible complex representation of a finite abelian group is one-dimensional, and the number of irreducible characters equals the group order.
conditions: G is a finite abelian group
conclusion: All irreducible characters of G have dimension 1 and there are |G| of them.
typical_uses: Construct character tables for cyclic and finite abelian groups.
Show commuting finite-order matrices are simultaneously diagonalizable over C.
common_misuses: Applying one-dimensionality to nonabelian groups.
Counting conjugacy classes incorrectly for abelian groups.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Permutation character counts fixed points
statement: For the permutation representation associated to a finite G-set S, the character value at g equals the number of elements of S fixed by g.
conditions: G acts on a finite nonempty set S
rho is the associated permutation representation
conclusion: chi(g)=|Fix_S(g)|.
typical_uses: Compute characters of group actions.
Decompose permutation representations.
common_misuses: Counting orbits instead of fixed points for each group element.
Using the formula for a representation that is not a permutation representation.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Regular representation decomposition
statement: The regular representation of a finite group has character |G| at the identity and 0 elsewhere, and decomposes as the direct sum of irreducible representations with multiplicity equal to their dimensions.
conditions: G is a finite group
chi_1,...,chi_r are the irreducible characters with dimensions d_i
conclusion: rho_reg ~= direct_sum_i d_i rho_i and |G|=sum_i d_i^2.
typical_uses: Check completeness of a character table.
Compute unknown irreducible dimensions.
common_misuses: Giving each irreducible multiplicity one.
Forgetting the identity value of the regular character is |G|.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Schur lemma
statement: A G-invariant linear map between irreducible complex representations is either zero or an isomorphism; a G-invariant endomorphism of an irreducible representation is scalar.
conditions: V and W are irreducible complex representations of G
T:V->W is G-invariant
conclusion: T=0 or T is an isomorphism; if V=W then T=cI.
typical_uses: Prove orthogonality of irreducible characters.
Classify intertwiners between irreducible representations.
common_misuses: Applying scalar-endomorphism conclusion to reducible representations.
Forgetting T must commute with the group action.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Kernel and image of an intertwiner are invariant
statement: If T is a G-invariant linear map between representations, then ker(T) and im(T) are G-invariant subspaces.
conditions: T:V->W is linear
T(gv)=gT(v) for all g and v
conclusion: ker(T) is G-invariant in V and im(T) is G-invariant in W.
typical_uses: Prove irreducible maps are injective or surjective.
Find invariant subspaces from equivariant maps.
common_misuses: Using kernel/image invariance for maps that do not commute with the action.
Confusing ordinary linear maps with intertwiners.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Rational algebraic integers are integers
statement: A rational number is an algebraic integer if and only if it is an ordinary integer.
conditions: a is a rational number
conclusion: a is an algebraic integer iff a is in Z.
typical_uses: Rule out nonintegral rational coefficients as algebraic integers.
Repair proofs that confuse algebraic numbers with algebraic integers.
common_misuses: Assuming every algebraic number is an algebraic integer.
Checking a nonmonic polynomial instead of a monic one.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Integers in a quadratic field
statement: For Q(delta) with delta^2=d square-free, the algebraic integers are Z[delta] when d is 2 or 3 mod 4, and Z[(1+delta)/2] when d is 1 mod 4.
conditions: d is square-free
delta^2=d
conclusion: The ring of integers is determined by d modulo 4 as stated.
typical_uses: Choose the correct integer ring for quadratic-field ideal computations.
Detect invalid use of Z[sqrt(d)] when d is 1 mod 4.
common_misuses: Forgetting half-integers in the d=1 mod 4 case.
Using the real square root notation without tracking the abstract conjugate.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Generators of a product ideal
statement: If ideals A and B are generated by a_i and b_j, then the product ideal AB is generated by all products a_i b_j; in particular, (a)(b)=(ab).
conditions: A and B are ideals in a ring R
conclusion: AB=(a_i b_j for all i,j).
typical_uses: Compute products of ideals from generators.
Refine element factorizations into ideal factorizations.
common_misuses: Multiplying only matching generators instead of all pairwise products.
Assuming every product ideal is principal.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Ideal times conjugate is principal
statement: In the ring of integers of an imaginary quadratic field, the product of a nonzero ideal A with its conjugate is a principal ideal generated by a positive integer.
conditions: R is the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic field
A is a nonzero ideal of R
conclusion: A conjugate(A)=(n) for some positive integer n.
typical_uses: Define and compute norms of ideals.
Prove cancellation and divisibility properties for ideals.
common_misuses: Applying the statement in an arbitrary non-Dedekind ring.
Using an order smaller than the full ring of integers.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Cancellation for nonzero ideals
statement: For nonzero ideals in the ring of integers of an imaginary quadratic field, AB=AC implies B=C; inclusion AB subset AC is equivalent to B subset C.
conditions: R is the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic field
A,B,C are nonzero ideals of R
conclusion: Multiplication by A can be cancelled in equalities and inclusions of ideals.
typical_uses: Prove uniqueness of ideal factorizations.
Translate ideal containment into divisibility.
common_misuses: Cancelling zero ideals or arbitrary subsets.
Assuming ideal cancellation in rings where the required hypotheses fail.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Prime ideal criteria
statement: An ideal P is prime iff R/P is an integral domain, equivalently ab in P forces a in P or b in P. Every maximal ideal is prime.
conditions: P is an ideal of a ring R
conclusion: Prime ideal membership and quotient-domain criteria are equivalent.
typical_uses: Check prime ideals through quotient rings.
Lift divisibility arguments from elements to ideals.
common_misuses: Confusing prime ideals with prime elements.
Assuming every prime ideal is maximal in arbitrary rings.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Unique factorization of ideals
statement: In the ring of integers of an imaginary quadratic field, every proper ideal factors as a product of prime ideals, uniquely up to order.
conditions: R is the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic field
I is a proper ideal of R
conclusion: I has a unique prime-ideal factorization up to ordering.
typical_uses: Replace failed unique factorization of elements by ideal factorization.
Compute class groups from prime ideals.
common_misuses: Claiming unique factorization of elements from unique factorization of ideals without checking principal ideals.
Applying the theorem to arbitrary rings.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: PID, UFD, and trivial class group
statement: For the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic field, being a UFD, being a PID, and having trivial class group are equivalent.
conditions: R is the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic field
conclusion: R is a UFD iff R is a PID iff the class group is trivial.
typical_uses: Use class group computations to decide unique factorization.
Repair proofs that confuse element factorization and ideal principality.
common_misuses: Assuming UFD implies PID in arbitrary domains.
Using the class group before defining ideal classes and principal ideals.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Prime splitting in quadratic integer rings
statement: For an imaginary quadratic integer ring, an integer prime p either remains prime or factors as P conjugate(P). In the d=2 or 3 mod 4 case, p remains prime iff x^2-d is irreducible over F_p; in the d=1 mod 4 case, use x^2-x+(1-d)/4.
conditions: R is the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic field
p is an integer prime
conclusion: Splitting behavior is decided by irreducibility of the corresponding quadratic polynomial modulo p.
typical_uses: Find prime ideal factors for class group computations.
Determine ramification and splitting in examples.
common_misuses: Testing reducibility over Q instead of F_p.
Using x^2-d in the d=1 mod 4 case.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Ideal norm is multiplicative
statement: For nonzero ideals in an imaginary quadratic integer ring, the ideal norm satisfies N(AB)=N(A)N(B), equals the index [R:A], and agrees with element norm on principal ideals.
conditions: R is the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic field
A and B are nonzero ideals
conclusion: N(AB)=N(A)N(B), N(A)=[R:A], and N((a))=N(a).
typical_uses: Compute ideal classes and relations from element norms.
Bound possible class group generators.
common_misuses: Confusing ideal norm with vector length.
Ignoring that principal ideal norm uses absolute field norm conventions.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Class group finite generation by small prime ideals
statement: In an imaginary quadratic integer ring, every ideal class has a representative with bounded norm, and the class group is finite and generated by prime ideal classes with prime norm below the standard bound.
conditions: R is the ring of integers in an imaginary quadratic field
conclusion: The class group is finite and can be generated by finitely many small prime ideals.
typical_uses: Compute class groups by checking finitely many primes.
Prove class number finiteness in this setting.
common_misuses: Assuming all small primes contribute nontrivially.
Forgetting primes that remain prime have trivial ideal class contribution.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Quartic Galois group and resolvent cubic
statement: For an irreducible quartic, the resolvent cubic helps distinguish possible transitive subgroups of S4: if the resolvent is irreducible, the Galois group has order divisible by 3; if it has roots in the base field, the group is constrained to the corresponding S4/A4/D4/C4/D2 cases.
conditions: f is an irreducible quartic over F
g is its resolvent cubic
K is the splitting field
conclusion: The factorization pattern of g restricts the Galois group of f.
typical_uses: Determine possible quartic Galois groups.
Repair proofs that use only the discriminant for quartics.
common_misuses: Treating the resolvent alone as always determining the exact group.
Applying quartic subgroup tests to reducible quartics.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Quadratic subfield of prime cyclotomic field
statement: For odd prime p, the unique quadratic subfield of Q(zeta_p) is Q(sqrt(p)) if p is 1 mod 4 and Q(sqrt(-p)) if p is 3 mod 4.
conditions: p is an odd prime
zeta_p is a primitive pth root of unity
conclusion: The quadratic subfield of Q(zeta_p) is determined by p modulo 4.
typical_uses: Identify intermediate fields in prime cyclotomic extensions.
Use Galois correspondence for the index-two subgroup of F_p^*.
common_misuses: Forgetting the sign change when p is 3 mod 4.
Assuming there are multiple quadratic subfields in the prime cyclotomic case.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Solvability by radicals via field chains
statement: A complex number is solvable over F by radicals iff it lies in a tower of fields built by adjoining radicals, equivalently in a tower whose successive extensions are Galois of prime degree after suitable enlargement.
conditions: F is a subfield of C
alpha is a complex number
conclusion: Radical solvability can be tested through a suitable chain of prime-degree Galois extensions.
typical_uses: Connect radical formulas to Galois-theoretic solvability.
Set up impossibility proofs for equations by radicals.
common_misuses: Confusing constructibility by square roots with arbitrary radical solvability.
Assuming a displayed radical expression has no branch ambiguity.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Equations of degree at most four are solvable by radicals
statement: Every root of a polynomial of degree at most four over a subfield of C is solvable by radicals over that field.
conditions: f is a polynomial over F
deg(f)<=4
F is a subfield of C
conclusion: Each root of f is solvable over F by radicals.

Separate quartic solvability from the general quintic obstruction.

Ignoring irreducibility and splitting-field distinctions in Galois group computations.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Quintics with A5 or S5 Galois group are not solvable
statement: If an irreducible quintic over F has Galois group A5 or S5, then its roots are not solvable by radicals over F.

F is a subfield of C
Gal(f/F) is A5 or S5
conclusion: The roots of f are not solvable over F by radicals.
typical_uses: Prove specific quintic equations are not solvable by radicals.
Diagnose invalid radical-solution claims for generic quintics.

Forgetting that the theorem requires a Galois group computation.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Character values are sums of roots of unity
statement: If g has finite order k and rho has dimension d, then chi(g) is a sum of d kth roots of unity; also chi(g^{-1}) is the complex conjugate of chi(g).

g in G has order k

Compute character values from eigenvalues of finite-order operators.

Ignoring inverse conjugacy when checking a table.

name: Character inner product by conjugacy classes
statement: The character inner product can be computed by summing over conjugacy classes: <chi,psi>=(1/|G|) sum_i |C_i| chi(g_i) conjugate(psi(g_i)).
conditions: G is finite
C_i are conjugacy classes with representatives g_i
chi and psi are class functions
conclusion: The class-size weighted formula computes the Hermitian inner product.

Test irreducibility by checking <chi,chi>=1.

Using unweighted row dot products unless all classes have size 1.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Number of irreducible representations
statement: For a finite group over C, the number of irreducible representations equals the number of conjugacy classes, and the squared dimensions of the irreducibles sum to |G|.

rho_i are representatives of irreducible complex representations

Check whether a character table has the right number of rows.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Characters determine finite complex representations

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Kernel of a one-dimensional character
statement: A one-dimensional character is a group homomorphism G->C^*. Its kernel is the union of conjugacy classes on which the character value is 1.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: S3 irreducible character pattern

classes are ordered as identity, 3-cycles, transpositions

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Cyclic group character table pattern
statement: For a cyclic group C_n generated by x, the irreducible complex characters are one-dimensional and send x to the n distinct nth roots of unity.

source: Artin Algebra, Second Edition; rewritten seed rule
name: Smith normal form pivot reduction step
statement: In the integer Smith normal form algorithm, move a nonzero entry of smallest absolute value to the pivot position, use Euclidean row and column operations to clear the pivot row and column, and restart if a smaller remainder appears.
conditions: A is a nonzero integer matrix
Only unimodular row and column operations are allowed
conclusion: Repeated pivot reduction terminates and leads toward diagonal invariant factors.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Addition rule

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Conditional product rule
statement: P(A intersection B)=P(A|B)P(B)=P(B|A)P(A) whenever the conditioning probability is positive.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Bayes rule
statement: For a partition {B_i} with positive probabilities, P(B_j|A)=P(A|B_j)P(B_j)/sum_i P(A|B_i)P(B_i).

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Law of total probability
statement: If {B_i} partitions the sample space, then P(A)=sum_i P(A|B_i)P(B_i).

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Indicator variable method

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Variance of independent sums
statement: If X_i are pairwise independent with finite variances, Var(sum_i X_i)=sum_i Var(X_i).

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Convolution formula
statement: For independent discrete X,Y, P(X+Y=n)=sum_k P(X=k)P(Y=n-k); continuous densities convolve by an integral.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

statement: For iid variables with finite mean and variance, the sample average converges in probability to the common mean.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Chebyshev inequality
statement: For finite-variance X, P(|X-E X|>=a) <= Var(X)/a^2 for a>0.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

statement: For iid variables with mean mu and variance sigma squared>0, the standardized sum converges in distribution to a standard normal law.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Probability generating function

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Transition matrix and Markov property

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

conclusion: The hitting probability solves the harmonic recurrence h_i=p h_{i+1}+q h_{i-1} with boundary values 0 and 1.

common_misuses: Using the biased formula at p=q without taking the limit.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

Confusing the random variable with a particular realized outcome.

Singleton outcomes are elements of the sample space.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

m(omega) >= 0 for every omega in Omega.
The sum of m(omega) over Omega is 1.
E is a subset of Omega.

Check whether a proposed finite probability model is normalized.

Using equal masses without justifying uniformity.
Summing over outcomes outside the event.

A finite sum over the empty event is 0.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Basic finite probability properties

A, B, E, and F are events in Omega.

Detect invalid addition of probabilities for overlapping events.

If E is a subset of F, then F is the disjoint union of E and F minus E.

A intersect B and A intersect B complement are disjoint and union to A.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Uniform distribution on a finite sample space

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

m(omega) >= 0 for every omega.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Criterion for independent events
statement: Two events are independent exactly when the probability of their intersection equals the product of their probabilities, with zero-probability events treated as independent by convention in the text.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Mutual independence of events
statement: A finite family of events is mutually independent when every subfamily has intersection probability equal to the product of its member probabilities.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Joint discrete random variable
statement: Given random variables X1,...,Xn, their joint random variable takes ordered tuples of their values, with joint probabilities assigned on the Cartesian product of the individual value sets.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Independent discrete random variables

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Independent trials process

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Bayes formula for finite hypotheses
statement: For a finite partition of hypotheses, the posterior probability of a hypothesis given evidence equals its prior times likelihood divided by the total likelihood-weighted prior mass.

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Standard continuous density patterns

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Density transformation by monotone change of variable
statement: For a one-to-one differentiable transformation Y=phi(X), the density of Y is obtained by evaluating the density of X at the inverse image and multiplying by the absolute derivative of the inverse.

Y=phi(X).

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Inverse CDF sampling

source: Grinstead and Snell, Introduction to Probability.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Expected value of a discrete random variable

The series sum_x x m(x) converges absolutely.

statement: For random variables with finite expectations, expectation is additive and homogeneous; independence is not required.

name: Expectation of product under independence

name: Conditional expectation on an event
statement: For an event F with positive probability, the conditional expectation of X given F is the expectation computed using the conditional distribution restricted to F.

State si has transition probability pii=1 for absorption.
